lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hey, welcome back. Episode two of Introduction to Chinese Economy. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And I'm Leo. And last time you promised this one would be juicy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I did, and I stand by it. Today is China's institutions. And it starts with a puzzle.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Go.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So, growth before nineteen seventy eight was about four point four percent a year. After nineteen seventy eight, about nine and a half. And the standard story in economics says growth needs certain things first. Secure property rights, then good market institutions, then growth.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Right, the textbook recipe.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The textbook recipe. But early reform China didn't really have those. Weak private property protection. Contracts that weren't reliably enforced. Very limited financial markets. And yet it grew like crazy.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So partial reforms, rapid growth, and then a big question mark.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. The main question is, how did China create growth incentives without fully adopting Western style market institutions?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the answer?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The one line answer on the slide is, institutions shape incentives. And China created incentives through decentralization, competition, and experimentation.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, unpack that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The core idea comes from the economist Chenggang Xu. He calls it regional decentralized authoritarianism. R D A.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That's a mouthful.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It is, but it's actually simple. Political centralization plus economic decentralization. The center controls the politics. Who gets appointed, who gets promoted, who gets fired, and the big strategic policies. But local governments are responsible for the economy. Developing their region, allocating resources, implementing policy.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So Beijing holds the leash, but the locals do the running.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's a really good way to say it. And there are two reasons for this setup. An information problem and an incentive problem. Local governments simply know more about local resources, local firms, local conditions. And the center needs some way to motivate local officials to actually use that knowledge.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the government has a bunch of layers, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Five levels. Central, then province, then prefecture, then county, then township. And most of the economic management happens below the center. Chinese local governments are way more involved in the economy than in most countries. Attracting investment, building infrastructure, picking industries, rolling out reforms.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. So where did this setup come from? Did someone design it in nineteen seventy eight?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No, and that's one of the most interesting parts. It goes way back. In imperial China, the Emperor appointed local officials, but those officials had a lot of discretion over local affairs.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Because, what, the Emperor couldn't send a text message?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ha. Pretty much. Communication and transport were slow. The local guy knew what was going on, so you had to let him decide things. Central control of people, local discretion over policy.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And there's a paper about provincial capitals that I honestly didn't expect in an economics lecture.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Bai and Jia, twenty twenty three. I love this one. The question is, how did the central government choose where to put each provincial capital?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the answer is math.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The answer is basically logistics. A provincial capital does two jobs. It's the administrative center of the province, and it's the relay point between the central government and all the prefectures. Think about taxes. You have to haul tax revenue from each prefecture to the provincial capital, and then send a share of it on to the national capital. Moving stuff is expensive, and the cost grows with distance.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So you pick the city that minimizes total hauling.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. They call it hierarchical distance. Distance to all the prefectures, weighted by how much tax each one produces, plus distance to the national capital, weighted by the share you send up. And that share is about thirty percent in the Song and Ming dynasties, and about twenty percent in the Qing and in modern China.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And it works?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It predicts the actual capitals really well. The takeaway is that the shape of the Chinese state was built around the problem of governing a huge territory with bad information.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, then the communists come in, and they copy the Soviet Union.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Early nineteen fifties, a Soviet style planned economy. Central planning, state ownership, resources allocated by administrators. Very centralized.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that has the usual problems.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Weak incentives, slow adjustment, no room for experiments. And here the lecture brings in Hayek.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: The famous critique.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah. Hayek's point is that economic knowledge is scattered. It's in millions of heads. Some of it is tacit, you can't even write it down. And it keeps changing. So no central planner can ever collect it all. In a market, prices do that job. A price rises, and suddenly everyone knows something is scarce without anyone writing a report.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, but then the Great Leap Forward.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right, and this is the twist. During the Great Leap Forward, from nineteen fifty eight to nineteen sixty two, there was a huge, kind of accidental, decentralization. Central ministries handed control of tons of enterprises down to local governments.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Accidental how?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It wasn't a plan to build a market economy. But the result was lots of fairly self contained regional economies, where local governments ran factories, assigned labor, decided investment. And those capabilities survived.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So in nineteen seventy eight...

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In nineteen seventy eight China was still a planned economy, but local governments already controlled a lot of real economic resources. The line I'd remember is, reform didn't create local governments as economic actors. It empowered existing ones.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Oh, that's a good line.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And then why gradual? Two kinds of uncertainty. Political uncertainty, people resisting reform, ideological fights. And economic uncertainty. Nobody knew what would happen, nobody had market experience. So the solution was, experiment first, reform later. Keep the old system, add new experiments next to it, and scale up whatever works.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, so we have the structure. How does it actually produce growth?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three mechanisms. Regional competition, policy experimentation, and local governments acting like entrepreneurs. Let's start with competition.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: The tournament.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The tournament. Local officials aren't rewarded with profits. They're rewarded with promotion. And their performance is judged relative to other regions. So, roughly, your chance of promotion depends on your growth minus everyone else's growth.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: It's like a sales team where only the top performer gets the corner office.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly that. Better growth, higher promotion chances, more effort.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Why GDP though? Why not something else?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: After nineteen seventy eight the national line was, take economic development as the central task. Leaders had visited Europe and the US and saw how far behind Chinese industry was. And GDP growth is easy to observe, easy to measure, and easy to compare across regions.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Even if what you really want to reward is effort and ability.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right, but you can't see those directly. So GDP becomes the signal.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And why does this tournament work so well in China specifically?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Four reasons. One, the center has strong personnel control. Higher levels appoint, promote, and dismiss, all the way down. The slide calls it the nested cadre system. Two, officials really care about promotion. Three, regions look alike. Most have farms, factories, services, so comparing them is fair. And four, local governments control important resources, so they can actually move the needle.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And it worked.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It did. Local governments went out and attracted investment, built roads, supported firms, tried reforms. They became development agents. And the data show better economic performance really is linked to promotion.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: But I'm guessing there's a catch.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's always a catch. The professor asks, what if local governments get money that has nothing to do with economic performance?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Land.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Land. This is Chen and Kung, twenty sixteen. In nineteen ninety eight there was a land reform. All non farm land is owned by the state. Only local governments can convert farmland into industrial or commercial land. Private users get seventy year use rights. And local governments get to keep all the money from land sales.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That's a lot of money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An enormous amount. From nineteen ninety eight, county governments started relying on land income in a big way. And the paper's idea is a political resource curse.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Like the oil curse, but for land?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. With the oil curse, governments that get easy oil money depend less on their citizens. Here, officials with easy land money depend less on growing the economy. So land revenue weakens the link between growth and promotion.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: How do they test it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They look at county party secretaries from nineteen ninety nine to two thousand eight. About seventeen and a half thousand county years, more than four thousand three hundred officials. And they code what happens to each one. Promoted is three, moved sideways or stayed is two, retired is one, and terminated, meaning corruption, resignation, or death, is zero.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And they regress that on land revenue and growth.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the interaction of the two, which is the key part. The question is whether growth matters less for promotion when land revenue is high.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: But there's an obvious problem. An ambitious official probably sells more land and also gets promoted more.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes, endogeneity. And there's reverse causality too. Promotion decisions are basically known a year ahead, which could change how much land you sell in your last year. Or an official who knows they won't be promoted might just sell everything.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So instruments.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Two clever ones. The first uses geography. Some counties have lots of land that's too steep to build on. In those places land supply is tight, so when national interest rates fall, land prices jump more. So they interact steepness with interest rate changes. The second interacts that same steepness with house prices in the provincial capital, as a demand shock from the nearby big city.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the result?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Land revenue reduces the importance of GDP growth in promotion. And then they look at where the money goes. First, signaling. Officials spend land money on visible image projects, city construction and land development, timed right before they're evaluated. Short terms, under five years, make them pretty short sighted.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Shiny buildings right before the review.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Basically. Second, corruption. Land revenue goes with higher administrative spending and a bigger bureaucracy. And third, who benefits most? Officials who are politically connected to their bosses, same birthplace or used to work in the prefecture government. And officials over forty four, who are unlikely to be promoted anyway.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So the people with the least incentive to grow the economy benefit most from land money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Adverse selection. Okay, second mechanism. Experimentation.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Crossing the river by feeling the stones.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the one. Experiment, evaluate, expand. And why let local governments run the experiments? They have local information, that's Hayek again. They have incentives to solve problems, thanks to the promotion system. If an experiment fails, the damage stays local. And if it works, it can spread.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the classic example is Xiaogang village.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. Before reform, farming was collective, so effort didn't really pay off for anyone personally. In nineteen seventy eight, farmers in Xiaogang secretly split the land among households and signed a contract. Secretly, because it was risky.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And productivity exploded.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It did. And the central government later legalized it and spread it nationwide. That's the household responsibility system. The adoption chart shows counties switching over really fast, and agricultural productivity jumping.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the second example is Special Economic Zones.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Foreign investment was politically touchy. So instead of opening the whole country, China opened a few experimental zones. Shenzhen being the famous one. They offered lower taxes and tax holidays, duty free imported inputs, permission for joint ventures, land use rights, flexible labor. And when it worked, it spread to other cities.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, but this all sounds a little too good. Experiment, it works, scale it up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And that's exactly the question the lecture asks. Are experiments actually informative? This is Wang and Yang, twenty twenty one. The problem is that the regions picked for experiments aren't average regions.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Selection bias.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Selection bias. They find three things. First, experimental sites are positively selected. They're better off to begin with, and the choice is shaped by the career incentives of the local party secretary. Second, those regions put extra effort into the reform, because they're being watched. And third, when the policy is rolled out to everyone else, it works much less well.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Is there an example?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Local fiscal empowerment. Provinces were allowed to skip the prefecture level and manage counties directly, which gave counties more fiscal power. More than eleven hundred counties were picked between two thousand three and twenty thirteen. And the early experimental counties did better than the ones that got it later. So if you judged the policy from the pilots, you'd overestimate it.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: It's like testing a diet on people who are already super motivated.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Perfect analogy. And the professor adds one more thing. The pilot regions might be winning partly by pulling migrants and investment away from other regions. So the national gain could be smaller still.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, so we've got competition, we've got experiments. What breaks?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The last part is about limits. The big idea is the multi task problem. If you judge people on one measurable target, they focus on that target and neglect everything else.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Teaching to the test.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly, teaching to the test. Governments care about growth, but also the environment, social welfare, public services. Early on, everyone agreed growth came first, so a GDP target mobilized everyone. But after decades of fast growth, you get pollution, inequality, wasteful investment, fiscal risks. And the old incentive system doesn't fit anymore.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then the pollution paper.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He and coauthors, twenty twenty. So the center started adding environmental targets. For example, the tenth five year plan, two thousand one to two thousand five, required national water pollution to fall by ten percent, measured as C O D, chemical oxygen demand. Those targets were passed down to provinces, then prefectures and counties, and built into promotion decisions.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, sounds like a fix.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Here's the catch. Water quality is measured at monitoring stations along rivers. And a station only picks up pollution from upstream.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Oh no. So you only clean up upstream of the station.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Officials cracked down hard on firms just upstream of a monitoring station, and went easy on firms just downstream. The authors compare firms right on either side of a station, which is a regression discontinuity design. And they find upstream firms in polluting industries lose productivity. Their T F P drops. Non polluting industries, no effect.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So the measured pollution falls, but the river downstream doesn't care.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The slide calls it strategic compliance. You hit the target, not necessarily the goal.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. Three things to remember from today?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One. China's core institution is regional decentralized authoritarianism. Political centralization plus economic decentralization, with roots going back to imperial China and an accidental push from the Great Leap Forward. Two. It generated growth through a promotion tournament among local officials and through local policy experiments, like Xiaogang and the Special Economic Zones. Three. The same institutions created new problems. Land finance weakened growth incentives, pilot experiments were biased by selection, and pollution targets led to gaming.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And one practical thing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Oh, right. Group presentations are in the last three classes, groups of about six, twenty minutes each. And send your group's top three paper choices to the T A by December first.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Don't forget that one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Don't forget that one. See you next time.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: See you.
